Quantinuum’s logical qubits on Helios failed as rarely as five times per million rounds of error correction, a record. 

Error correction spreads each logical qubit’s information across a group of physical qubits so that errors in individual qubits can be detected and corrected. Code distance sets the size of that group, and on Helios each step up in distance cut errors by a factor of 12 on average. But breaking Bitcoin’s ECC would still require error rates several orders of magnitude lower.

posts.title: A recent US staff letter states that, based on the facts presented, a specific network token qualifies as a digital commodity but does not confirm that it is not a security.
posts.author: Lunis Partners
posts.snippet:
A recent US staff letter states that, based on the facts presented, a specific network token qualifies as a digital commodity but does not confirm that it is not a security.

The Division of Corporation Finance (Office of Chief Counsel) at the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) replied on 3 November 2026 to a request from Digital Asset Holdings, LLC. Relying on the representations, staff stated that Canton Coin “is a ‘digital commodity,’ as that term is described in the Interpretation,” meaning the SEC’s March 2026 release (Rel. 33-11412).

Lunis rating: Monitor. This is a staff opinion on a single token and does not impose obligations on crypto-asset service providers.

1. The relief. Staff will not recommend enforcement for programmatic minting without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act.

2. The gap. Digital Asset Holdings sought confirmation that the token “is not itself a ‘security’.” Staff did not give it and stated the response “does not express any legal conclusion on the issues presented.”

3. The conditions. “These positions are based on the representations made to the Division in your letter.” Different facts may lead to a different answer.

4. The two points. Staff singled out two points. First, the token’s value arises from the network’s programmatic operation, together with market supply and demand, not from profits expected from others’ essential managerial work. Second, the Interpretation defines no ‘central par.’n.

Lunis’s view: Platforms and custodians holding this token may include the response and its conditions in their asset files. Other networks receive an example of staff considerations but no regulatory relief.

Briefing attached.

#DigitalAssets #SEC #CryptoRegulation
posts.reason: Detailed analysis of SEC token classification by a legal firm speaks directly to token classification expertise and CASP/compliance concerns, and would engage GCs and compliance leads considering regulatory implications.

comments.text: Worth flagging the gap the letter leaves open: staff confirm Canton Coin fits the digital commodity description but explicitly decline to say it is not a security. In the EU this would simply be the classification question MiCAR already forces on every token - utility, e-money or ART - and no amount of US staff comfort changes that analysis for an EU-facing CASP.

Given staff tied the relief to the specific representations in the Digital Asset Holdings letter, how much weight do compliance teams think this actually carries for other networks with similar but not identical tokenomics?

We see the EU mirror of this constantly: clients want a one-line answer on whether a token 'is a security' or 'is MiCAR-compliant', and the honest answer is always conditional on the facts as represented, not a blanket clearance.

posts.title: 🔎 Pacioli.ai doesn't ask you to trust one checker. It asks a network of independent nodes to agree, in public.
posts.author: Anil R
posts.snippet:
🔎 Pacioli.ai doesn't ask you to trust one checker. It asks a network of independent nodes to agree, in public.
Inside the PVN (Pacioli Validating Node) network of Pacioli, Auditchain Labs AG's disclosure automation and external validation protocol: who runs the nodes checking machine-readable filings, what they stake, and who writes the rules.
Who Can Run One
Any qualified licensee can operate a PVN: physical machines in real locations, the DePIN (Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Network) layer under the filings. Operators stake AUDT to activate a node, and disclosure creators stake too. The rulebook is voted on: AUDT holders govern the maximum PVN count, staking requirements, reward splits and consensus thresholds. Filings needing a legal or audit opinion before release can go to a cohort: lawyers for whitepapers, licensed accountants for financial statements, under an EVC (External Validation Contract).
The Job
Pacioli's homepage gives the node one line of work: it "reads, understands and provides proof of compliance for regulatory disclosures." A filing arrives with its taxonomy model, and the request is recorded on-chain from the moment of submission. Each PVN runs the Pacioli AI Agent, which scans for requests and races the other nodes: first to finish a correct check takes the primary reward, and nodes reaching the same result corroborate it and share.
Nine Ways to Fail
The output is a pass-or-fail state condition across nine categories, from Proof of Reserves and report mathematics to disclosure mechanics and Process Controls. On the open protocol, corroborators' published starting share of structured-disclosure validation rewards is 18%. Every result publishes to the Pacioli Explorer, color-coded by validation status, and updated filings build a longitudinal compliance record anyone can read. Supported schemes include MiCAR (Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation), IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) and US GAAP.
Fine Print
The design above is as Pacioli publishes it on its own pages. Staking amounts and reward terms are governance parameters set by AUDT holder vote; the published splits are starting allocations, not fixed terms. A pass records that a filing met its model's rules; acceptance remains each regulator's own decision.
In Plain English
Instead of one hired checker, a filing goes to a crowd of independent operators running the same rulebook. They race, they must agree, and the scoreboard is public.
Why This Is Bullish
Instead of resting on one desk, the check is spread across independent, staked operators, and every result lands in public, where the record keeps building.

posts.title: Remember the CLARITY Act and the uncertainty around its vote a few months ago? At that time, the news created negative sentiment in the crypto market.
posts.author: Hamza Kiyani
posts.snippet:
Remember the CLARITY Act and the uncertainty around its vote a few months ago? At that time, the news created negative sentiment in the crypto market.

Now, after the Democrats gained seats in the U.S. Midterm Elections, the future of this bill could become more uncertain.

This could also create challenges for Trump’s plan to make the United States the global hub for crypto.

First, what is the CLARITY Act?

In simple words, the CLARITY Act is a bill designed to give the crypto industry clear rules and legal protection in the United States.

Right now, there is a lot of confusion about crypto regulations, especially regarding which digital assets should be controlled by the SEC and which should fall under the CFTC.

The crypto industry needs clear rules so businesses and investors know what is allowed and what is not.

What could happen if the CLARITY Act gets delayed?

Here are three possible impacts:

1. More Delays in Crypto Regulations

Republicans may need more support from Democrats to pass this bill. With Democrats gaining more political power, getting enough votes could become difficult.

2. Stricter Crypto Regulations

We could see stricter rules for crypto exchanges, stablecoins, and other digital assets. This could make it harder for crypto companies to operate in the United States.

3. Less Confidence from Big Investors

Banks and large financial institutions may become more careful about investing in crypto because of unclear regulations. This could slow down institutional money entering the market.

MY PERSONAL TAKE – DR CRYPTO

In my opinion, this development could make the future of the crypto industry more challenging, especially in the United States.

But let me make one thing clear: This does NOT mean crypto is dead!

Bitcoin is not going anywhere. The crypto industry will continue to grow and develop.

However, regulations play a very important role in this industry. They affect how businesses operate, how much institutional money enters the market, and how comfortable big investors feel investing in crypto.

Trump wants to make America the global crypto hub, but achieving this goal will require proper regulations, political support, and cooperation between both parties.

And this is where things could become difficult.

Remember, crypto is not just about Bitcoin going up or down. It’s about the future of the entire financial industry.

As investors, we need to watch both the charts and the political developments because decisions made in Washington can have a major impact on the crypto market.

Sometimes, the biggest moves in crypto don’t start on the charts. They start in Washington.

— Dr Crypto

posts.title: 🚨Plot twist of the year in crypto cards: KAST just canceled the token.
posts.author: Vladyslav Serdiukov 🇺🇦
posts.snippet:
🚨Plot twist of the year in crypto cards: KAST just canceled the token.

After months of points farming, premium memberships, and “TGE in 2026” energy, the points are turning into something called Pioneer Units instead. Non-tradable. Non-transferable. No equity. No guaranteed cash-out. Just… vibes and future possibilities.

It’s the crypto equivalent of being promised a house party and getting a polite “we’ll send you a calendar invite someday” email.

The points-to-token meta has been the main growth hack for a lot of neobanks and cards. KAST was one of the bigger ones playing it.

I believe one of the main reasons of going away from this system was regulation, legal opinions, and the track record of every previous card token dumping are starting to outweigh the short-term hype.

Of course, the actual product keeps humming along.

However, KAST lost a big piece of loyal audience, which will now find another better card service, like https://jamcard.io/ for example. 

Anyone else still holding points in something right now?
posts.reason: Token cancellation due to regulatory and legal concerns is a substantive discussion point about tokenomics and regulation that would interest founders evaluating token strategy.

comments.text: The shift from tradable points to a non-transferable 'Pioneer Units' structure looks less like a product pivot and more like a deliberate retreat from anything that could be read as an offer of a transferable, tradable right - which is exactly the territory MiCAR's e-money and asset-referenced token definitions were built to catch.
Do you think this is a genuine regulatory read, or just a convenient excuse to quietly shelve a TGE that was never going to clear scrutiny anyway?

We've reviewed a fair number of points-to-token programmes at the tokenomics stage, and the ones that survive contact with legal review almost always end up looking like this - stripped of tradability, equity and guaranteed cash-out, because that's what keeps them outside the regulated perimeter.

posts.title: Last week in Washington, D.C., I had the opportunity to serve as an American Intellectual Property Law Association (AIPLA) student reporter and attend an insightful discussion: on
posts.author: Laillah R.
posts.snippet:
Last week in Washington, D.C., I had the opportunity to serve as an American Intellectual Property Law Association (AIPLA) student reporter and attend an insightful discussion: on 'AI as a Patent Drafter, Prosecutor, and Strategist'.
The panel featured Ian Schick, PhD, Esq of Paximal (moderator), Micheal Binns of Pulsis, Steve Gong of Google, and Toni Nijm of Anaqua—accomplished professionals whose backgrounds span engineering, science, intellectual property, and legal practice. Their collective experience across law firms and technology-driven businesses reflects the increasingly important intersection of technical expertise and legal innovation. They are forging new paths and delivering high-impact work that is helping reshape the future of the legal landscape.

Several takeaways particularly resonated with me:

1.⚡Efficiency is only part of the equation.
AI-assisted patent drafting is demonstrating the potential to improve work-product quality while reducing time and costs. However, the real measure of success is whether the resulting patent application effectively protects the underlying innovation and advances the client's business objectives.

2.  🛠️ AI creates both opportunities and challenges for the next generation of attorneys.
An especially interesting discussion centered on Google's research examining AI's impact on patent attorney skill development. Experienced practitioners may strengthen their skills through AI-assisted work, while early-career professionals may not develop the same foundational competencies without independent practice. This raises an important question: How do we leverage AI without compromising the development of future legal talent?

3.   📋 Patent strategy is becoming increasingly data driven.
AI is creating new opportunities to evaluate patent portfolios, identify commercially valuable assets, and align intellectual property protection with broader business strategies. The objective is not necessarily to obtain more patents, but to secure the right protection for the right innovations.

4.  🧠 AI adoption requires more than purchasing technology.
There is a distinction between experimenting with AI, incorporating it into individual workflows, and fundamentally transforming how legal services are delivered. The greatest opportunity lies in rethinking existing processes—not simply automating them.

5.  👤 Human judgment remains essential.
AI can assist with drafting, analysis, and identifying potential issues. However, claim strategy, prosecution decisions, legal accountability, and business judgment require meaningful human oversight.

#ArtificialIntelligence #PatentLaw #IntellectualProperty #LegalTech #Innovation #AIPLA #FutureOfLaw
posts.reason: Substantive discussion of AI's impact on patent drafting, attorney skill development and patent strategy is directly relevant to Lemur Legal's deep tech and IP practice.

The data-driven portfolio point is the one worth sitting with: as AI makes it cheaper to generate applications, the real differentiator shifts to deciding which inventions are commercially worth protecting at all, which is ultimately a business strategy judgment, not a drafting one.

posts.title: Receiving one approval does not necessarily mean every regulatory obligation has been satisfied.
posts.author: Nabi Niazi
posts.snippet:
Receiving one approval does not necessarily mean every regulatory obligation has been satisfied.
Residential development can involve several overlapping sets of rules. Zoning may establish the permitted use and building form, while construction codes, fire safety provisions, environmental requirements, and historic preservation controls address other aspects of the project.
Each set of regulations serves a different purpose. A property may be suitable for a particular use under zoning but still be subject to additional conditions before construction or occupancy can proceed.
This is especially important when a project involves an existing building, a historically significant property, or a location with environmental constraints.
A useful early review identifies the agencies and regulations that may be relevant to the property. It also clarifies which approvals are required and which issues need further investigation.
For builders, this can help avoid treating a preliminary zoning conclusion as a guarantee that the entire project is ready for construction.
For real estate agents, it helps distinguish between a property's apparent potential and a development proposal that has been checked against the relevant requirements.
The exact legal relationship between different regulations depends on the jurisdiction and the specific circumstances. Where multiple rules apply, compliance with one should never be assumed to excuse noncompliance with another.
This is why regulatory coordination belongs near the beginning of project planning. Discovering an additional requirement after drawings are complete can lead to redesign, delays, or unexpected costs.
A sound development assessment asks not only whether the intended project is permitted, but also what other rules must be satisfied before the project can move forward.

New episode of Get Sh*t Done with Keire Murphy on the corporate capture of the state, with a focus on the US.

Everyone agrees the state needs to deliver better. The question is how. One answer, very loud in the US right now, is run the state like a business and let the people with money run the show. We argue the opposite. You can’t have a functioning democracy without a strong state, and a strong state is one that’s independent of concentrated corporate interests, not one handed over to them.

Markets left to themselves don’t produce competition. They produce concentration. Ten corporate groups take about 30 per cent of all profit in the US. That economic power becomes political power, and it compounds. Ireland isn’t immune: a state that depends on a handful of tech and pharma firms for its revenue is structurally exposed to their interests, whatever the intentions.

So what do you do about it? Taxation matters, but wealth taxes and progressive corporate taxes are less about raising revenue than about limiting the power of the people at the top. 

The bigger lever is stopping wealth concentrating in the first place: antitrust, transparency and disclosure, taking on the wealth defence industry in law and accounting, and rebuilding worker power through collective bargaining.

As I say to my students, if you’re really pro market, you should be anti big business. If you believe in markets, corporate concentration should worry you as much as it worries anyone on the left.

posts.title: The same week the Dutch defence ministry chose a European sovereign cloud, the Council's first draft of Europe's sovereign cloud law took defence out of the risk assessments that t
posts.author: Bert Desmet
posts.snippet:
The same week the Dutch defence ministry chose a European sovereign cloud, the Council's first draft of Europe's sovereign cloud law took defence out of the risk assessments that trigger it.

In September I forecasted two things. Defence would leave through an exemption, and everyone else would classify down, because member states grade their own services. The only check on that was the Commission's power to overrule their grading. The Irish compromise text replaces it with recommendations.

The rest points the same way. Public bodies get 18 months to migrate instead of 12, with further extensions possible, and only where their own risk assessment says they must. Metadata and telemetry may leave the EU at lower levels. The Commission loses its power to extend assessments to critical private companies, while member states pull utilities such as water and electricity in themselves.

To be fair, fines would go up, and one of the experts quoted on the text calls the changes not that significant overall. It is also still a draft that will be further discussed on 10 November.

The direction matters more than the size. Sovereignty in this draft is something a ministry chooses. The Dutch chose it. Nothing in the text would have required them to.
I am keeping my bet. The top tier ends up smaller than designed, and defence is the largest workload outside it.

Fridecast, Fridays. Forecasts on European tech and sovereignty, with dates attached.

#DigitalSovereignty #CloudSovereignty #Fridecast #CADA
posts.reason: Detailed analysis of EU cloud sovereignty law and defence exemptions—directly relevant to Lemur's defence/dual-use export control practice and regulatory audience.

comments.text: The Commission losing the power to overrule member state self-grading is the structural change that matters most here — a recommendation regime means the top tier becomes whatever each ministry is willing to admit it needs, which is a much weaker sovereignty guarantee than the original design.

If defence exits through the exemption and utilities get pulled in by member states directly, does the draft still give the Commission any residual tool to challenge an obviously under-graded critical private company, or is that gone entirely?

We see this same dynamic in dual-use export control classification — self-assessment regimes with only a discretionary override tend to drift toward the lowest compliant tier unless something forces a recalibration.

posts.title: I can’t imagine how tough it must be to be young and looking for work right now.
posts.author: Dereck Maruma
posts.snippet:
I can’t imagine how tough it must be to be young and looking for work right now.

For years, young people were told where the future was. Get into tech. Go into finance. Learn to code. Those were the “safe” careers, the exciting ones, the ones that would set you up.

So a lot of them did exactly that. They picked the courses, did the degrees, built the CVs.
And now those same industries are quietly needing them less.

That’s a horrible feeling. Doing everything you were told, then finding the door you were pointed towards is slowly closing.

The data backs it up. New research from BCG shows jobs for 18 to 24 year olds in UK tech and finance have dropped 22% since 2022. That’s around 45,000 roles.

The jobs haven’t gone. They’ve moved (well this is what I'm telling myself).

Since 2019, the fastest growth in jobs for young people has been in construction, transport and logistics, and arts and recreation.

The problem is, most young people have no idea. The Milburn review found fewer than 1 in 5 remember anyone talking to them about apprenticeships.

That’s the whole reason we started HIYA. There are brilliant careers out there that young people just never get shown.

And they’re not finding them on job boards. Their parent's don't know about them and They’re still getting the same generic careers advice on TikTok and Instagram. If your roles aren’t there, they might as well not exist.

This year we've worked across law enforcement, defence, publishing, transport and logistics, children's services and adult care and one thing I can say is, it's not that people don't want your jobs they just don't know they exist.

So I’ll ask: which role in your organisation would a young person jump at, if they only knew it existed?

posts.title: Dimension | Artificial Intelligence (AI) | Quantum Computing |
posts.author: Deepak M.
posts.snippet:
Dimension | Artificial Intelligence (AI) | Quantum Computing |
|---|---|---|
| Core Mechanism | Binary bits (0s and 1s) running complex algorithms | Qubits using superposition and entanglement |
| Primary Strength | Pattern recognition, prediction, and automation | Solving massive, multi-variable calculations simultaneously |
| Job Market Impact | Automates routine coding, content, and data tasks | Creates demand for quantum physicists and algorithm architects |
| Security Impact | Detects threats faster, but powers realistic deepfakes | Breaks current RSA encryption, requiring quantum-safe cryptography |
| Earth & Climate | Optimizes power grids and tracks deforestation | Simulates molecules to build carbon-capture materials |
1. The Shift in Developer and IT Jobs
If you are a software engineer or data scientist today, your focus is likely on Python, PyTorch, and cloud infrastructure. AI is already writing boilerplate code, pushing developers to become system architects rather than just coders. Quantum computing takes this a step further. It will not make traditional developers obsolete, but it will split the tech workforce. We will need a new breed of engineers who understand quantum logic gates and probabilistic outcomes rather than simple if-else statements. R&D teams that start upskilling their developers in quantum-ready frameworks today will lead the market tomorrow.
2. Earth Security and Planetary Survival
When we talk about "Earth security," we are looking at two things: our climate and our critical global infrastructure. Classical AI is great at analyzing satellite data to predict weather patterns, but it hits a wall when trying to simulate nature at an atomic level. Quantum computers operate on the exact same laws of physics as the molecules they are trying to simulate. By combining Quantum and AI, researchers can design new fertilizers that do not pollute soil, invent high-capacity batteries in weeks instead of decades, and secure global food and water supply chains against climate shocks.
3. Cybersecurity: The Ultimate Lock and the Ultimate Key
Right now, our banking systems, defence networks, and personal data rely on encryption that would take a traditional supercomputer thousands of years to crack. A mature quantum computer could shatter that encryption in minutes. Meanwhile, AI is already being used by bad actors to launch automated, hyper-personalized phishing attacks. The future of digital security depends on "Post-Quantum Cryptography." Organizations cannot wait for the quantum era to arrive before upgrading their security protocols; by then, their encrypted data will already be compromised.
4. Human Behaviour and Trust
Technology changes faster than human psychology. AI has already blurred the line between what is real and what is generated, making people second-guess the videos they see, the voices they hear, and the messages they read. We are becoming naturally more sceptical—and sometimes more isolated—as digital interactions replace human ones. When quantum-powered AI starts predicting human choices, consumer habits, and even health outcomes with near-perfect accuracy, we will face a massive ethical test. Where does helpful prediction end, and where does the loss of human free will begin?
We do not need to fear these technologies, but we do need to respect their scale. AI is teaching machines how to think like us; Quantum Computing will teach machines how to solve problems we cannot even comprehend yet.
How is your team preparing for the next decade of computing? Are you focusing solely on AI, or is Quantum on your radar too? Let’s discuss in the comments.

posts.title: The countries winning digital assets are solving a legal problem, not a blockchain problem.
posts.author: Marco Kowalewski
posts.snippet:
The countries winning digital assets are solving a legal problem, not a blockchain problem.

The technology can already move a token from one wallet to another in seconds.

The harder question is:

What legally moved with it?

Imagine a token represents an interest in a €50M property.

I send that token to you.

The blockchain can prove the transaction happened.

But the important questions start afterwards.

Did legal ownership of the underlying asset actually transfer?

Would a court recognize you as the owner?

What happens if the issuer becomes insolvent?

Are you holding property rights — or simply a contractual claim against a company?

Which jurisdiction's law applies if:

→ the asset is in Germany

→ the issuer is in Switzerland

→ the platform operates from Dubai

→ the buyer is in Singapore?

The blockchain may have technical finality.

That doesn't automatically create legal finality.

And I think this distinction will increasingly separate serious digital-asset markets from experiments.

The countries that attract institutional capital will need more than crypto-friendly regulation.

They need the legal system to answer very practical questions:

What does the token legally represent?

When does ownership transfer?

Which records are authoritative?

How are token holders treated in insolvency?

Can the asset be pledged as collateral?

Can courts enforce the rights attached to it?

How do digital records interact with existing registries?

Because institutional investors don't just need to know that a transaction cannot be reversed on-chain.

They need to know that their rights cannot disappear off-chain.

This changes how I think about competition between jurisdictions.

The winner may not be the country with:

The fastest blockchain.

The most Web3 startups.

Or even the lowest taxes.

It may be the jurisdiction that creates the clearest bridge between:

code → contract → ownership → enforcement.

Blockchain can tell us who holds the token.

Law determines what holding that token actually means.

And until those two systems agree, we haven't fully digitized ownership.

We've digitized only the record of it.

🔁 Repost to help founders avoid costly mistakes

posts.title: "Why should an unfunded startup pay more for compliance in India than its parent pays in the UK?"
posts.author: Avil Rakshith Salins
posts.snippet:
"Why should an unfunded startup pay more for compliance in India than its parent pays in the UK?"

A founder asked me this on a call today, and I didn't have a good answer.

Her company was incorporated in India in 2024. It is a research-stage startup with zero turnover and about Rs. 4 lakh a year in cash flow, funded mostly from the founder's own pocket while a funding round closes. Because its holding company is abroad, the law treats it very differently from an Indian-owned startup of the same size:

- A subsidiary can never be a "small company" under Section 2(85), whatever its size.
- So Rule 9B applies: mandatory ISIN and dematerialisation of shares.
- The cost of the ISIN alone is about Rs. 50,000 in the first year (depository plus RTA) and about Rs. 23,600 every year after that, plus half-yearly PAS-6 returns.
- The deadline had already passed, and none of her earlier advisors had told her about it.

The law isn't unclear here. My concern is whether it is proportionate. Unlisted public companies that are wholly owned subsidiaries are exempt under Rule 9A(11). 

Private companies have no equivalent exemption. An Indian-owned startup of the same size is exempt as a small company.

A size-based exemption, or a lower fee slab for early-stage foreign-owned startups, would go a long way.

To fellow professionals: tell clients about obligations like this at incorporation, not two years later. A missed compliance is far more expensive than the advice would have been.
#CompanySecretary #Startups #Compliance #Dematerialisation #EaseOfDoingBusiness #FDI
posts.reason: Detailed, expert discussion of Indian subsidiary compliance for startups with foreign parents—directly addresses founder compliance pain and lack of proportionate regulation, speaking to GCs and compliance leads.

Have you seen MCA move at all on a size-based exemption for Rule 9B, or does the foreign-subsidiary exclusion look fairly entrenched for now?

We see the cross-border version of this constantly - founders structuring with a foreign holding company for investor reasons without anyone flagging the compliance cost that triggers on day one, not two years in.

Nobody signed. Something did.

On October 29, roughly six billion dollars left Binance's hot wallets in under four hours — the largest theft of digital assets on record. On Tuesday the exchange published how.

It is not a story about crypto. It is a story about a tampered installer found through a search result, a job interview for a company that does not exist, an internal AI tool that gave attackers reach across a team, a permission token left on a laptop — and a signing service that was made to sign "outside the normal withdrawal process." Binance's words.

New in The Board-Ready Brief: what actually happened, what it is not (nobody's AI went rogue; no bank was touched), what Binance got right in the hours after, and what to do before Monday — eight steps for the business, five for the household.

Our founding client said it on Tuesday morning, hours before the report dropped: the question is not whether difficult times will come, but whether the operator can navigate them when they do. If your organization has any way for money to leave without a named person approving that specific transaction, you have a smaller version of the same door.

A crypto token buyback funded by a Wall Street money-market fund?

It's an unlikely pairing, and one that raises a few questions.

World Liberty Financial has announced a new buyback program for $WLFI, with funding potentially coming from income generated by reserves backing its USD1 stablecoin.

And those reserves have included something you might not expect: Fidelity government money-market funds.

Think about that for a second.

People hold USD1. The assets backing it can generate income through traditional financial instruments. And some of that income could eventually be used to buy WLFI tokens.

The arrangement reveals just how closely traditional finance and crypto token economics are becoming intertwined.

Yet the financial mechanics behind it remain far from clear..

How much money will actually be allocated to buybacks?

How regularly will those purchases happen?

And will the income generated by a growing stablecoin business translate into meaningful value for WLFI holders?

Because there's an important distinction between a business earning money and its token capturing that value.

The buyback announcement gives us a possible connection between the two. It doesn't yet tell us how much money will flow through it.

Our latest Ravel investigation looks at the USD1 reserve structure, Fidelity's role, and the economics behind WLFI's new plan.

comments.text: The distinction you draw at the end is the one that matters legally too - income generated by reserve assets accruing to the issuer is one thing, but unless the token terms create an enforceable claim to that income, a buyback is a discretionary market action, not a value-capture right attached to the token.

Your crypto white paper has 40 pages. Nice graphics, detailed tokenomics and a roadmap that looks promising. Unfortunately, MiCA isn't particularly impressed by any of that.

We still come across projects that assume having a white paper means they've taken care of the legal side of their token launch. But a document written to attract investors or explain a project isn't necessarily a MiCA-compliant crypto-asset white paper. And adding a legal disclaimer at the bottom won't magically turn it into one either.

MiCA has specific disclosure requirements, depending on the type of crypto-asset and the applicable regulatory framework. There are also rules around responsibility for the information, notification and publication. The good news? You don't necessarily have to throw your existing document away. It may be a useful starting point. But someone needs to establish what's missing, what needs to change and whether a MiCA white paper is required in the first place.

We help crypto projects with that process, from the initial legal assessment through drafting and regulatory notification.

💡 A white paper can explain your project beautifully and still fail to meet the legal requirements.

posts.author: Siva Prasad

🚨 CRAFTY FALCON: When AI Becomes a Force Multiplier for Financial Cybercrime
India's BFSI ecosystem is facing an evolving threat: AI-assisted cyberattacks designed not just to compromise systems, but to steal money.
On November 4, 2026, CERT-In's financial-sector response team (CSIRT-Fin) issued advisory CIAD-2026-0058, identifying CRAFTY FALCON, an active threat actor targeting India's BFSI and cryptocurrency ecosystem.
🔴 What makes this campaign concerning?
CRAFTY FALCON focuses on unauthorized financial transactions by abusing legitimate payment, disbursement, and merchant settlement APIs.
Key findings:
🔹 AI-assisted operations: Reported use of ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn, and CyberStrikeAI.
🔹 Initial access: Exploiting internet-facing applications, exposed APIs, stolen credentials, hardcoded tokens, and compromised source repositories.
🔹 Financial API abuse: Directly invoking payment APIs to bypass application-level controls.
🔹 Micro-transaction testing: Using small transactions (reportedly around ₹1) to validate unauthorized transfers before attempting larger amounts.
🔹 Crypto targeting: Stealing wallet keys and draining funds from cryptocurrency exchanges and virtual-asset service providers.
🔹 Evasion: Deleting logs, tampering with endpoint security, and rotating infrastructure.
⚠️ Attribution consideration:
CRAFTY FALCON is a CERT-In tracking designation. Its operators, country of origin, and potential state sponsorship remain unconfirmed. The use of publicly available AI tools does not establish attribution.
🛡️ Defensive priorities:
Enforce MFA and eliminate long-lived static API credentials.
Monitor unusual payment, payout, and settlement API activity.
Implement transaction limits and dual-approval mechanisms.
Separate production from development and testing environments.
Monitor suspicious beneficiary creation and micro-transactions.
Strengthen source-code, CI/CD, and application security.
Maintain continuous monitoring, including weekends and holidays.
My key takeaway:
The real concern is the combination of autonomous offensive tooling, compromised application infrastructure, and legitimate financial APIs.
Organizations cannot rely only on perimeter security or API gateway controls. Identity security, application integrity, transaction authorization, and continuous monitoring must work together.
The next generation of financial cyberattacks may not need to break the payment system. They may simply abuse the trust already built into it.

posts.title: The CBN is getting more serious about how crypto operates in Nigeria.
posts.author: Racheal Oyedepo
posts.snippet:
The CBN is getting more serious about how crypto operates in Nigeria.

Yesterday, the Central Bank of Nigeria released its Regulations for the Operations of Non-Security Virtual Assets in Nigeria.

The new framework covers stablecoins, Deposit Money Tokens (DMTs), virtual asset service providers and other related activities.

But here's what caught my attention.

The regulation goes beyond simply allowing crypto-related businesses to operate. It introduces requirements around licensing, minimum capital, reserve backing, liquidity, cybersecurity, customer protection and even how token issuers manage their reserves.

In other words, operating a virtual asset business in Nigeria could become a lot more demanding.

I think we're entering a different phase of crypto adoption in Nigeria.

The question is no longer just about whether the government recognises digital assets. It's increasingly about who gets to issue them, how they operate and what standards they must meet.

My question now is: 

Will these regulations make Nigeria's crypto ecosystem safer and more credible, or will the cost of compliance make it harder for smaller Web3 businesses and startups to survive?

I'm particularly interested in what founders and people building in the Nigerian Web3 ecosystem think.

• WorkOS: acesso não autorizado e uma framework ofensiva assistida por IA identificada.
• Northflank: uso indevido de AI API keys; recomendada rotação de secrets.
• LLMJacking: credenciais cloud roubadas geraram >US$100 mil em consumo fraudulento de IA num dia e quase US$1 milhão acumulado num caso.
• Cisco ASA/FTD: exploração activa de falha no SSL VPN capaz de causar indisponibilidade.
• Zyxel GS1900: quase 1.000 switches em 48 países comprometidos via zero-day.
• Synology: ransomware contra NAS desactualizados através de vulnerabilidade já corrigida.
• DreamHost: atacantes ficaram ~2 meses no File Manager, expondo credenciais FTP/SFTP e sessões webmail.
• DigiCert: sistema interno exposto à Internet; dados de clientes e alguns documentos de identificação potencialmente expostos.
• NIKKE: launcher oficial para PC comprometido para distribuir malware.
• XCPE: mais de 1,3 milhões de dispositivos Android transformados numa botnet.
• Crafty Falcon: campanha contra fintechs e exchanges com IA a automatizar partes da intrusão.

A OpenAI disponibilizou ainda o GPT-6 Cyber de forma restrita para investigação defensiva, com capacidade cibernética classificada como “Critical”.
Não é um ataque. É um sinal de até onde a IA já chegou.

O ciberataque já não termina no ecrã.
Pode mexer no dinheiro, desligar redes e alterar equipamentos físicos.
E agentes de IA começam a reconhecer alvos, procurar vulnerabilidades e testar caminhos de ataque a uma velocidade impossível para equipas humanas.
Mais coisas ligadas. Mais dependência digital. Ataques mais automatizados.

DISTOPIA - “Lugar hipotético onde se vive sob sistemas opressores, autoritários, de privação, perda ou desespero; antiutopia.”

A maior distopia em que vivemos não é ter problemas, mas comprar a narrativa de que o nosso sofrimento é único e que a solução estaria em virar o quintal dos outros.

Houve um momento muito recente em que o projeto para o Brasil era, literalmente, uma queima de estoque: estávamos na prateleira de liquidação, prestes a aceitar o destino de sermos uma colônia dócil e submissa do EUA.

Escapamos por um triz de nos tornarmos o puxadinho mais ensolarado de Washington.
Enquanto a gente se afogava no complexo de vira-lata, acreditando que a grama do vizinho era mais verde, a realidade latino-americana tratou de mostrar que os milagres liberais também vêm com boleto e o recado de quem vai pagar essa conta.

Argentina: O laboratório de choque mais radical apostou todas as fichas na motosserra. Conseguiu avanços na estabilização macroeconômica e no controle da inflação, mas a conta social continua pesando. Depois de uma queda expressiva, a pobreza voltou a subir, enquanto o consumo e o poder de compra seguem sob pressão.

Chile: O antigo oásis neoliberal, apresentado durante décadas como modelo a ser seguido, mas a desaceleração, os gargalos de produtividade e as desigualdades persistentes expõem os limites de um modelo que, por muito tempo, foi vendido como receita universal de sucesso.

Paraguai: O tigre latino-americano dos discursos cresce, atrai investimentos e apresenta números macroeconômicos expressivos. Mas há um detalhe que costuma desaparecer nas apresentações de PowerPoint: cerca de 62% dos trabalhadores estão na informalidade e o principal banco do país quebrou do dia pra noite, deixamos milhares sem sequer saber como irão pagar suas contas ou comprar comida.

A diferença é que nós pisamos no freio na beira do abismo #uffa

O Brasil é pesado, complexo e grande demais para caber no papel de colônia ou para adotar receitas que tratam seres humanos como números descartáveis.

E alguns números ajudam a desmontar a narrativa de um país condenado: 

Desemprego na menor média anual da série histórica, renda real do trabalhador em patamar recorde e uma economia que continua produzindo resultados apesar de seus enormes desafios.

Isso não significa que esteja tudo bem. 

Significa que reconhecer problemas não exige fechar os olhos para os avanços. E que serviços essenciais, proteção social e direitos trabalhistas não são simplesmente "custos" a serem eliminados numa planilha. São parte da estrutura que impede o desenvolvimento de se transformar em um moedor de gente.

A verdadeira virada de chave foi perceber que soberania não se pede licença, e desenvolvimento de verdade não existe sem qualidade de vida e autonomia para quem vive aqui.

No fim das contas, não adianta ter uma economia bonita na apresentação para investidores se a população continua sendo figurante na própria história.

posts.title: En Puerto Rico, para la mitad de los dueños de restaurantes, la luz ya cuesta más que la comida.
posts.author: Jose David Castro Zabarain

En Puerto Rico, para la mitad de los dueños de restaurantes, la luz ya cuesta más que la comida.

Un estudio de Inteligencia Económica para la Asociación de Restaurantes de Puerto Rico (Asore) encuestó a 898 establecimientos entre el 15 de septiembre y el 14 de octubre. Algunos resultados:

→ 35% de los dueños encuestados está considerando cerrar.
→ 66% opera con un margen menor a 8%. Y 17% opera con pérdida.
→ Para 51%, la luz es su principal costo de operación. Le siguen, de lejos, la comida (19.1%) y la empleomanía (12.8%).

La presidenta de Asore, Sonia Navarro, lo dijo claro: un restaurante debería tener como gasto principal la comida o su gente, no la electricidad.

Lo que me deja pensando como chef y operador: con márgenes de un dígito, un costo que no controlas puede decidir quién sigue abierto. Y no hay receta que baje la tarifa eléctrica.

Lo que sí controlas es qué tan bien conoces tus números. Por sucursal, no en total:
1. Costo primo: comida más mano de obra.
2. Ocupación y servicios: renta, luz, agua.
3. Todo lo demás.

Y luego la pregunta incómoda: si uno de tus costos fijos se dispara, ¿qué sucursal es la primera en dejar de ser rentable? ¿Lo sabes hoy, o lo vas a descubrir al cierre del mes?

Cuando el margen es de un dígito, no conocer tus números por sucursal no es un descuido. Es un riesgo.

¿Cuál es el costo que más ha subido en tu operación este año?

DeFi, Staking and the UK Regulatory Perimeter — Who Is Actually Responsible?

IssuE #22 of The Crypto Compliance Brief is now published.

This week, I'm looking at an area that continues to raise some interesting regulatory questions: decentralised finance (DeFi), staking and where regulatory responsibility sits when financial services are delivered through decentralised arrangements.

On 21 October, the FCA published two consultations, GC26/7 and CP26/36, providing further guidance on DeFi, financial crime risks and the UK cryptoasset regulatory perimeter.

One of the key questions is whether a protocol can genuinely be considered decentralised if an identifiable entity still controls its operations, governance or access arrangements.

And where does that leave firms providing staking services, technical infrastructure or access to decentralised protocols?

From a compliance perspective, these distinctions matter, particularly for firms preparing for the UK's new FSMA regime in October 2027.

In this week's edition, I also cover:
• The FCA's approach to DeFi and identifying regulatory responsibility.
• Staking arrangements and the distinction between technical activities and regulated financial services.
• ADGM's new crypto mining guidance and what it means for firms operating in Abu Dhabi.
• Next week's Digital Asset Summit (DAS) London, taking place on 10–11 November.

With both FCA consultations closing on 18 November, firms have a limited window to review the proposals and consider their implications.

For me, the important question is not simply whether a service uses decentralised technology, but who is ultimately responsible for the activities being carried out and the risks involved.

I'll also be following the discussions at DAS London next week, particularly around institutional DeFi, regulation and financial crime compliance.

posts.title: The UK’s experience: how preserving seized cryptoassets increased their value more than twelvefold.
posts.author: Pavlo Velykorechanin
posts.snippet:
The UK’s experience: how preserving seized cryptoassets increased their value more than twelvefold.

💰 In October 2018, London police seized devices containing the private keys to 61,000 bitcoins in the case of Zhimin Qian. At the time, the assets were worth approximately $400 million. Today, they are worth around $5 billion.

🔐 For eight years, law enforcement kept the private keys secure. The assets were neither sold nor moved. A London court is now deciding how to divide the increase in value between defrauded investors and the state.

🇺🇦 Ukraine is only beginning to develop its approach. In June, ARMA took seized cryptoassets under management for the first time: 8.3 million USDT. In August, a court authorised their sale because current legislation gives the agency no other tools for managing such assets. Under these rules, volatile cryptoassets would have to be sold at the prevailing market price, whatever the market conditions.

🇮🇹 European countries, meanwhile, are refining their approaches. Italy, for example, allows seized property to be sold before a confiscation ruling if keeping it incurs losses, and places crypto wallets under the management of a state fund.

⚖️ This experience shows that Ukraine needs more flexible mechanisms for managing seized digital assets, including the option to keep them secure without a mandatory sale.

📌 Read more about the case and my proposals for legislative changes in my column for SPEKA .

posts.title: PwC’s 5th Global Crypto Regulation Report is out and they frame 2027 as the year we question the architecture.
posts.author: Erwin Voloder, MES
posts.snippet:
PwC’s 5th Global Crypto Regulation Report is out and they frame 2027 as the year we question the architecture. 

2018 to 2022 was about defining the #asset. 2022 to 2025 was about the intermediary. 2025 to 2026 was about the #regime. The question now is whether a single #transaction can work end to end. 

Their example is a #tokenized fund share posted as collateral and settled in a stablecoin on a Sunday between counterparties in two jurisdictions. Each piece is regulated somewhere. Whether it works is another matter.

The eight trends they flag for 2027:

 1️⃣ Stablecoins sit alongside tokenized deposits and central bank money
 2️⃣ Tokenization shifts scrutiny onto market infrastructure, settlement finality and legal title
 3️⃣ Cross-border interoperability matters more as national regimes mature
 4️⃣ Tokenized equities show how far apart access models still are
 5️⃣ Supervision and enforcement become the real measure of maturity
 6️⃣ Banks and asset managers bring capital, conduct and resilience rules into digital assets
 7️⃣ DeFi, smart contracts and AI agents raise hard questions on accountability
 8️⃣ Perpetuals on equities, FX and commodities extend 24/7 leveraged trading to traditional assets

The idea I found most useful is what they call regulatory architecture debt. 

Pilot regimes, contractual bridges, special permissions and quiet supervisory tolerance help a product get started, but they also leave behind unresolved dependencies that get harder to carry as volumes grow. Meaning that a cheap licence can sit on top of a very expensive operating model.

By jurisdiction

 🇪🇺 EU. The MiCAR review report is due by 30 June 2027. MISP could move the most significant cross-border CASPs to direct ESMA supervision, convert the SFD into a regulation and lift the DLT Pilot ceiling. AMLR applies from 10 July 2027 and DAC8 reporting starts.

 🇺🇸 US. GENIUS goes live in January 2027. CLARITY stalled after the failed Senate vote in September, so the SEC and CFTC are filling the gap with interpretive releases, exemptions and no-action relief. 23 of 40 new OCC charter applications involved digital assets.

 🇬🇧 UK. The full FCA authorisation regime starts 25 October 2027 and the transitional application window closes 28 February 2027.

 🇸🇬 Singapore. MAS is consulting on letting banks treat some permissionless cryptoassets as Group 1.

 ✅ Standard setters. The Basel crypto standard has applied since January 2026 with a targeted review underway. FATF reports 83% of jurisdictions have passed Travel Rule laws, though implementation still lags.

One other interesting example they highlight is that of an #AI treasury agent who runs a trade no one checked. Who signed off? Whose licence? Can anyone stop it before settlement? Most regimes, and firms, haven’t asked.

Where are you seeing the biggest gaps?

Thank you Dr. Hagen Weiss for the flag!

posts.title: RWA: The real challenge isn't tokenisation. It's settlement.
posts.author: Rizwan ali
posts.snippet:
RWA: The real challenge isn't tokenisation. It's settlement.

Traditional asset transactions often involve fragmented records, multiple intermediaries, manual reconciliation, separate payment and delivery processes, and limited real-time visibility.

Tokenising an asset alone does not solve these operational challenges.

The real question is:

How do we connect verified assets, compliance controls, payment, delivery, and settlement into one coherent workflow?

The UK and EU are moving towards increasingly digital financial markets.

🇬🇧 The UK expects its DIGIT digital gilt pilot in Q1 2027, while the FCA's expanded cryptoasset regulatory regime begins on 25 October 2027.

🇪🇺 The EU's DLT Pilot Regime is evolving to support tokenised financial instruments and digital market infrastructure.

These developments highlight an important direction: the industry needs more than token issuance. It needs infrastructure capable of connecting the entire transaction lifecycle.

This is the problem NOVA is exploring.

Through our blockchain and infrastructure experiments, NOVA is developing and testing:

🔹 Asset and payment token integration
🔹 Pre-settlement verification and compliance gates
🔹 Atomic Delivery-versus-Payment (DvP) logic
🔹 Blockchain transaction monitoring and event-driven visibility
🔹 AI-assisted infrastructure and automation

Our Base blockchain demonstrations have explored payment-token settlement against tokenised asset delivery, including smart-contract execution and on-chain settlement evidence.

The objective is straightforward:

Move from fragmented workflows towards connected, verifiable transaction infrastructure.

Tokenisation creates the digital asset.

Settlement infrastructure connects the asset to the transaction.

And trust must be supported by verification, governance, and evidence—not just technology.

NOVA is building, testing, and learning towards that future.

Hace unos años, buena parte del debate sobre activos digitales se centraba en cómo integrar los criptoactivos en el sistema financiero. Hoy, la conversación es más amplia: cómo se moverá el dinero.

Desde mi experiencia jurídica y regulatoria en Brasil hasta mi reciente llegada a Madrid, he podido seguir de cerca esa evolución. La tokenización, las stablecoins y los depósitos bancarios tokenizados han pasado a ocupar un lugar cada vez más relevante en las conversaciones del sector.

Participar en MERGE Madrid fue una oportunidad para contrastar perspectivas sobre estos modelos y sus retos de interoperabilidad y compliance transfronterizo. Me llevo una reflexión que no se trata de encontrar una única solución, sino de entender qué instrumentos, marcos jurídicos e infraestructuras responden mejor a cada caso de uso.

La reciente publicación de Cinco Días refleja bien este cambio. La próxima etapa exigirá algo más que innovación tecnológica: seguridad jurídica, gobernanza y capacidad de conectar distintos modelos a escala global.

🇬🇧

A few years ago, much of the digital assets debate focused on how to integrate cryptoassets into the financial system. Today, the conversation is broader: how money itself will move.

From my legal and regulatory work in Brazil to my recent move to Madrid, I have had the opportunity to witness this evolution firsthand. Tokenization, stablecoins and tokenized bank deposits are becoming increasingly central to industry discussions.

Attending MERGE Madrid was an opportunity to exchange perspectives on these models and the challenges of interoperability and cross-border compliance. One takeaway stands out: the goal is not to find a single solution, but to understand which instruments, legal frameworks and infrastructures best serve each use case.

The recent Cinco Días article captures this shift. The next stage will require more than technological innovation: legal certainty, sound governance and the ability to connect different models globally.

posts.title: On Monday, EU finance ministers meet in Brussels and could decide what a can of nicotine pouches costs across Europe from 2028.
posts.author: Elliot White
posts.snippet:
On Monday, EU finance ministers meet in Brussels and could decide what a can of nicotine pouches costs across Europe from 2028.

On the table is a minimum EU excise rate for pouches, under the latest Irish presidency compromise:
- 2028 to 2029: 10% of retail price, or €30 per kg
- 2030 to 2031: 25%, or €40 per kg
- From 2032: 50%, or €50 per kg

For context, the European Commission's original proposal in July 2025 was €143 per kg. The number has come down a long way.

The catch: tax changes need all 27 member states to agree, and Sweden has been the holdout. Even if ministers agree a general approach on Monday, it still has to become law and be transposed in each country.

Why should a UK manufacturer care? Because if you make in the UK and sell into Europe, the shelf price there decides which brands survive. If you sell into the EU, now's the time to model your pricing at each tier.

I'll share what happens once the outcome is clear.

18+ only. Nicotine pouches contain nicotine, which is a highly addictive substance.

posts.title: Democrats took the House and the Senate. The next morning, Nvidia fell 3% and CoreWeave nearly 10%.
posts.author: Andrew Poddubny
posts.snippet:
Democrats took the House and the Senate. The next morning, Nvidia fell 3% and CoreWeave nearly 10%.

Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Apple went up. Apple gained about 5%.

Same election. Same AI. Opposite reactions. That split is the whole story - even if the broader tech market sold off a day later.

Will Democratic wins affect AI investment? Yes, but not the way the headlines frame it. They won’t stop the money. They will change where it goes.

Three reasons.

1. The bottleneck of AI has moved from the chip to the power socket.
Electricity bills and unwanted data centers became election issues. In an August poll, 57% of Texas voters opposed a data center in their community. Texas had already paused certain permits and grid connections, and the governor-elect campaigned on a broader moratorium. A federal data center moratorium bill has also been introduced.

None of this bans AI. All of it can make new infrastructure slower and more expensive to finance.

2. More oversight, without necessarily getting clearer rules.

Any new federal AI law would need the President’s signature. A Democratic-controlled Congress may increase scrutiny, while state governments move on their own.

That is a difficult kind of uncertainty for a project with a five-year payback — and a more manageable one for companies that already have compliance teams and infrastructure.

3. Divided government lowers macro risk, and the money has to go somewhere.

Bonds rallied, the dollar fell, and the Dow jumped after the vote. Then the Nasdaq fell 5.5% on Thursday. Investors aren’t simply making one bet on AI. They’re rethinking which parts of the buildout can produce real cash flow.

What to expect in the next 6 to 12 months:

More scrutiny of AI executives. State-level rules moving faster than federal ones. Neoclouds and second-tier suppliers facing a political risk premium. And one number I’m watching: hyperscaler capex guidance in the next earnings cycle. If they don’t cut spending, the “Democrats killed AI investment” story gets much harder to defend.

Now the part most people will disagree with.

The election did not create the selloff. The market had already started doubting the return on the AI buildout. Election day gave traders a story for an exit they were already considering.

And constrained compute could be the best thing to happen to the application layer. When GPUs and power get expensive and slow to build, value shifts to whoever does more with less. Efficient architecture over brute force. The right model in the right place instead of the biggest model everywhere.

The era of “throw more GPUs at it” is ending. That is not bad news for AI. It is bad news for a very specific way of investing in it.

SEBI has capped unhedged currency derivatives at a single USD 5 million notional across all INR pairs and recognised exchanges.

The 5 November 2026 circular aligns exchange-traded limits with RBI’s 10 October 2026 forex risk circular.

What changes:
• Domestic clients and FPIs may hold long or short INR currency-derivative positions without underlying exposure up to USD 5 million combined across exchanges
• FPI shorts in FCY-INR pairs must stay within USD 5 million
• FPI longs above USD 5 million need Indian equity or debt underlying (including MF units)
• Domestic clients above the cap follow RBI’s Master Direction on Risk Management and Inter-Bank Dealings
• Exchanges and clearing corporations must update systems, bye-laws and report status to SEBI

Why it matters: one market-wide unhedged limit instead of fragmented exchange stacks, with SEBI and RBI rules now pointing the same way.
